name: Enzacamene
lead: Enzacamene (4-methylbenzylidene camphor, 4-MBC) is a camphor-derived organic UVB filter that has been used in sunscreens and SPF-labelled skincare [1]. It has been the subject of endocrine-activity research, and it has been banned in cosmetics in the European Union (Regulation (EU) 2024/996), with further bans reported in the UK and China [1].

It remains permitted in some places, including Canada (up to 4%) and, per the source, Australia; it is not FDA-approved in the United States [1]. It is discussed in sunscreen-ingredient communities mainly in the context of ingredient safety and regional availability.
infobox: Not FDA-approved as a sunscreen active

paras: Enzacamene is a water-insoluble white crystalline solid that dissipates absorbed UV energy partly through cis-trans isomerisation; its low quantum yield for that process suggests other photochemical reactions occur, which is linked to limited photostability [1].

In vitro work reported estrogenic activity for several UV filters including 4-MBC, which displaced estradiol from estrogen receptor beta and increased uterine weight in immature rats [2]. Reporter-gene assays also examined 4-MBC interactions with estrogen, androgen and progesterone receptors [3]. Wikipedia reports rodent thyroid effects at higher doses [1].

A human study measured systemic absorption after whole-body topical application of benzophenone-3, octyl methoxycinnamate and 4-MBC, alongside reproductive hormone levels [4]. Another reported UV filters in human plasma and urine after repeated whole-body application [5]. 4-MBC has also been detected in human milk, with levels correlated with cosmetic use [6].

Studies have detected 4-MBC in wastewater, surface water and fish in Swiss lakes [7][8] and in surface waters in several countries [9]. A review of environmental effects of sunscreen ingredients discusses it among other filters [10].
No clinical trials of enzacamene as a cosmetic or sunscreen treatment were found. Human data consist of absorption and exposure studies [4][5][6] and a registered photopatch study of UV filters [11].

Denmark proposed warnings against use in children under 12 in 2001, and retailers there largely stopped selling products containing it [1]. The EU Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety concluded in 2022 that endocrine-disruption evidence was sufficient and genotoxicity data insufficient; the EU banned it in cosmetics in 2024, with products to be off the market by May 2026 [1]. The UK moved to prohibit it in 2026 and China removed it from permitted UV filters in January 2026, according to the same source [1]. Palau and Thailand national parks restrict it [1].

timeline.event: Danish authorities propose a voluntary warning against use on children under 12 [1].
EU SCCS opinion finds sufficient evidence of endocrine disruption [1].
EU bans 4-MBC in cosmetics via Regulation (EU) 2024/996 [1].
China removes it from permitted UV filters; UK regulations laid to prohibit it [1].

card.summary: Camphor-derived UVB sunscreen filter (4-MBC) now banned in EU cosmetics over endocrine-activity findings.
card.note: Banned in EU cosmetics (2024) and reportedly the UK and China; not FDA-approved.

quick.overview:
Enzacamene (4-MBC) is an organic UVB filter once used in sunscreens, especially in Europe. Regulators have since moved against it because of endocrine-activity research.

It is still permitted in some countries, such as Canada, while the EU has banned it in cosmetics and the US never approved it.
quick.mechanism: It absorbs UVB light and dissipates the energy partly through cis-trans isomerisation, though its photostability is described as limited.
quick.risks: Lab and animal studies reported estrogenic and thyroid effects, and human studies detected it in plasma, urine and milk. The EU SCCS found sufficient evidence of endocrine disruption in 2022.
